scenarios.title: Shadows on the Panels
scenarios.description: Your crew of four has landed near the Moon's **South Pole**. The Sun sits low in the sky, so a ridge's long shadow covers some solar panels. The battery is only half charged.

decisions.title: Start the science lab
decisions.explanation: Begin research now, using battery power.

decisions.title: Save power first
decisions.explanation: Pause research and let the panels recharge the battery.

fact.text: Near the Moon's South Pole, the Sun stays close to the horizon. Mountains and crater rims cast long shadows that move across the ground, so some spots get long stretches of sunlight while others stay dark.

scenarios.title: Dust on the Panels
scenarios.description: The automatic dust cleaner has stopped working. Dust blasted up by your lander's rocket engines is covering the solar panels, so they make less power.

decisions.title: Clean the panels by hand
decisions.explanation: Two astronauts go outside with brushes. Spacesuits use extra oxygen.

decisions.title: Leave the dust
decisions.explanation: Stay safe inside. The panels will make less power every day.
decisions.laterHint: Dusty panels make less power every day

fact.text: Moon dust is sharp and sticks to everything. NASA studies show that even a very thin layer of dust can cut a solar panel's power in half. In 2025, NASA's Electrodynamic Dust Shield used electricity to lift dust off surfaces on the Moon.

scenarios.title: Damaged Power Cable
scenarios.description: A small space rock crashed near the outpost. Bits of flying rock cut the main power cable that brings electricity from the solar panels.

decisions.title: Repair the cable
decisions.explanation: Two astronauts go outside to fix it. Spacesuits use extra oxygen.

decisions.title: Switch to the backup cable
decisions.explanation: Stay inside. The thin backup cable carries only half the power.
decisions.laterHint: The backup cable carries less power every day

fact.text: Space rocks still hit the Moon today. By comparing before-and-after pictures, NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter found over 200 new craters, about 3 to 43 meters wide, that formed while it was watching.

scenarios.title: Solar Storm Warning!
scenarios.description: Mission Control has spotted a burst of fast particles from the Sun heading your way. Two astronauts are outside collecting rock samples.

decisions.title: Go to the storm shelter
decisions.explanation: Come inside and hide behind the water tanks. Leave the rocks.

overrides.note: This storm had super-fast particles, but the water walls kept your crew safe.

decisions.title: Finish collecting samples
decisions.explanation: Stay out a little longer to finish the job, then come in.

overrides.note: This storm had super-fast particles that went right through the spacesuits.

fact.text: Water has lots of hydrogen, which is good at blocking space radiation, so NASA plans storm shelters surrounded by water containers. NASA estimates that astronauts caught on the Moon without shelter during the big solar storm of August 1972 would have received a dangerous dose.

scenarios.title: Oxygen from Moon Soil
scenarios.description: Your crew brought a test machine that melts Moon soil to pull out the oxygen hidden inside it. It makes fresh air, but it needs lots of electricity.

decisions.title: Run the oxygen machine
decisions.explanation: Melt one batch of Moon soil to make oxygen.

decisions.title: Keep it switched off
decisions.explanation: Save the electricity for the outpost.

fact.text: In 2025, NASA scientists at Kennedy Space Center melted fake Moon soil made on Earth at 1,700 °C (3,100 °F), then used electricity to pull pure oxygen out of it. It was a test on Earth: no machine makes oxygen on the Moon yet.

scenarios.title: Carbon Dioxide Alert
scenarios.description: The machine that removes carbon dioxide, the gas we breathe out, is almost full. If it stops, the air will become unsafe to breathe.

decisions.title: Use a spare filter canister
decisions.explanation: Swap in a fresh chemical canister. It can only be used once.

decisions.title: Bake the filters clean
decisions.explanation: Heat the filters so they can be reused. It uses lots of power.

fact.text: The Space Station's main carbon dioxide remover traps the gas in tiny crystals, then heats them so the gas escapes into space and the crystals can be used again. Lithium hydroxide canisters, used on Apollo and the Space Shuttle, are the backup. They get used up as they work.

scenarios.title: Final Countdown
scenarios.description: It's your last day before the trip home. There's time for one more experiment, or you can carefully pack the rock samples.

decisions.title: One last experiment
decisions.explanation: Run the lab one more time. It uses lots of power.

decisions.title: Pack up for the trip home
decisions.explanation: Seal the rock samples so they reach Earth safely.

fact.text: On Apollo 17 in 1972, astronauts spent about 22 hours exploring outside on three moonwalks and brought home about 110 kilograms of Moon rocks and soil.

flagDailyEffects.note: Dusty panels made only half their power.
The backup cable carried only half the power.

debriefTips.lifeSupport: Every spacewalk uses about two days of the crew's oxygen. Plan trips outside carefully!
debriefTips.power: Dust and a weak backup cable drain power every day. Fixing problems early keeps the battery healthy!
debriefTips.radiation: When a solar storm comes, go to the shelter right away. Water walls block the fast particles!
